newsitem.title: USA: US NAPM index rises strongly in November.
newsitem.headline: US NAPM index rises strongly in November.

text.p: A soft price index soothed market reaction to an otherwise stronger-than-expected National Association of Purchasing Management index, which was marked by gains in most components, analysts said.

"Generally speaking this was a vigorous report and puts the composite index at its highest reading since June," said William Sullivan, senior vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
"But the prices paid index suggests that we can continue to improve in overall activity and we need not disturb the inflation picture," Sullivan added.

The NAPM index rose to 52.7 in November from 50.2 in October, based on increases in production, new orders, supplier deliveries, inventories and employment. Economists in a Reuters survey had forecast a slight 0.6 percentage point rise in the index to 50.8 for November.
The prices paid index, meanwhile, fell to 45.9 from 47.1.

Some economists said the strength in NAPM was unlikely to spark spot revisions to fourth quarter economic outlooks. Indeed, Donald Fine, chief market analyst at Chase Asset Management, said the data was moderate and far from what he considers worrisome.

"By and large the data show what all the other numbers have shown," Fine said. "Moderate economic growth with little in the way of economic pressures. The number went up a little bit more and I stress the word little."

Nevertheless, Sullivan contended that some of the rally seen over the past two months was predicated on the notion that a manufacturing slowdown seen in September would be sustained through October and November. More vigorous manufacturing activity in November may ultimately give the fixed-income markets a reason to pause, he said.

Anthony Karydakis, senior financial market economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc, said it would take a string of stronger than expected manufacturing data to upend current positive market sentiment. He attached little significance to the marginally higher pace of manufacturing growth.
"It would take at least a couple more months (of strength) ... to (heighten concerns)," he said. "Even then, tentatively there would be a case of a sudden pickup in manufacturing but not right now."
Economists noted the U.S. Treasury market was fixated for good reason on the price component and emerged unscathed.

In further analysis, Karydakis said the second consecutive rise in the supplier delivery component may pique some interest given that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has been known to focus on it. But again he said a strong trend has yet to be established in the component, which rose to 51.5 in November versus 50.7 in October and 49.7 in September.
That trend probably won't happen, according to Merrill Lynch senior economist Cheryl Katz, who also predicted modest economic growth and low inflation for the fourth quarter.
"The rise in orders and backlog was most likely due to a jump in the electronic equipment sector, as observed in last week's durable goods report," Katz said in her daily economic commentary.
